summary.text: Japan is an island country in East Asia, lying in the Pacific Ocean off the eastern coast of the Asian continent. It is an archipelago of thousands of islands, of which the four largest are Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku. Tokyo is its capital and largest city.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: Tokyo, which is also the country's largest city.

facts.label: Geography
facts.value: An archipelago in the Pacific Ocean whose four largest islands — Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku — make up about 97% of its land area.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: Roughly 123 million people, among the most populous countries in the world.

facts.label: Highest point
facts.value: Mount Fuji, at 3,776 metres (12,388 feet), is the highest mountain in Japan.

media.alt: Satellite view of the Japanese archipelago, showing the four main islands from north to south: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.
media.attribution: NASA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Satellite image of Japan in April 2018

summary.text: Kyoto is a city on the island of Honshu in Japan and one of the country's oldest municipalities. Founded in 794 as Heian-kyo, it served as the imperial capital of Japan from then until the middle of the 19th century, and it remains a centre of traditional Japanese culture.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: Established in 794 as Heian-kyo, laid out on the model of the ancient Chinese capital of Chang'an.

facts.label: Former capital
facts.value: The imperial capital of Japan from its foundation in 794 until the mid-19th century.

sources.name: UNESCO — Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Several of its historic temples and gardens were collectively inscribed as the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto' in 1994.

sources.name: UNESCO — Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto

facts.label: Original name
facts.value: Heian-kyo, meaning 'peaceful/tranquil capital', established by Emperor Kanmu.

media.alt: The Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji), a gold-leaf-covered temple building reflected in its pond, in Kyoto, Japan.
media.attribution: Fg2 (released into the public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower between 1887 and 1889 for the 1889 Exposition Universelle.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: About 330 metres (1,083 feet) from base to tip.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Constructed from 1887 to 1889 by the company of engineer Gustave Eiffel.

facts.label: Record
facts.value: On completion it became the tallest human-made structure in the world, a title it held until the Chrysler Building was finished in 1930.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Stands on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France.

media.alt: The Eiffel Tower in Paris viewed from below against a clear sky, showing its wrought-iron lattice structure.
media.attribution: Photographer dedicated the work to the public domain under CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Mount Fuji is an active stratovolcano on the island of Honshu in Japan and the country's highest mountain. Known for its symmetrical conical form, it last erupted in the early 18th century and has long been a cultural icon of Japan.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: 3,776 metres (12,388 feet), the highest mountain in Japan.

facts.label: Last eruption
facts.value: Erupted most recently from 1707 to 1708.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013 as a cultural site.

sources.name: UNESCO — Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies on the island of Honshu, south-west of Tokyo near the Pacific coast.

media.alt: The snow-capped, symmetrical cone of Mount Fuji photographed from the International Space Station at an oblique angle.
media.attribution: NASA (public domain), astronaut photograph from the International Space Station, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — ISS-46 Mount Fuji, Japan.jpg

summary.text: Mont-Saint-Michel is a tidal island and commune in Normandy, France, crowned by a Gothic-style Benedictine abbey dedicated to the archangel St Michael. Set on a rocky islet amid vast sandbanks exposed to powerful tides, it was historically accessible to pilgrims only at low tide.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 as 'Mont-Saint-Michel and its Bay'.

facts.label: Abbey founded
facts.value: The abbey was founded in 966; the present buildings are mostly in the Gothic style.

sources.name: Wikipedia — List of World Heritage Sites in France

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: A tidal island on a rocky islet amid sandbanks between Normandy and Brittany, exposed to powerful tides.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: A commune in Normandy, north-western France.

media.alt: Mont-Saint-Michel rising from its bay, with the Benedictine abbey and spire crowning the rocky tidal island.
media.attribution: Photographer released the work into the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Grand Canyon is a steep-sided canyon carved by the Colorado River in the state of Arizona in the United States. Running for roughly 446 kilometres (277 miles) and reaching a depth of more than 1.6 kilometres (a mile), it exposes nearly two billion years of the Earth's geological history in its layered walls.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 446 kilometres (277 miles) long.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: Attains a depth of over 1.6 kilometres (about 1,857 metres, or more than a mile).

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: Carved by the Colorado River, which is thought to have established its course through the area roughly 5 to 6 million years ago.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Grand Canyon National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979.

media.alt: The Grand Canyon and the Colorado River in Arizona seen from an orbital vantage point, showing the branching canyon system cut into the Colorado Plateau.
media.attribution: NASA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel set on a mountain ridge in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, at about 2,430 metres (7,970 feet) above sea level. Built in the classical Inca dry-stone style, it is one of the most iconic surviving sites of the Inca civilization and a major archaeological site in the Americas.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Constructed around 1450 by the Inca, during the reign associated with the emperor Pachacuti.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: Sits at about 2,430 metres (7,970 feet) on a ridge above the Urubamba River valley.

facts.label: Construction style
facts.value: Built in the classical Inca style using finely crafted dry-stone walls, including structures such as the Temple of the Sun and the Intihuatana stone.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 as the Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu.

sources.name: UNESCO — Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu

media.alt: The stone terraces and buildings of Machu Picchu on a mountain ridge, partly veiled in mist, with steep Andean peaks behind.
media.attribution: Willian Justen de Vasconcellos, via Unsplash / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Machu Picchu In Mist (Unsplash).jpg

summary.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching for over 2,300 kilometres (1,400 miles) in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland, Australia. Composed of thousands of individual reefs and hundreds of islands built by tiny coral polyps, it is the largest single structure made by living organisms and can be seen from space.

facts.label: Extent
facts.value: Stretches for more than 2,300 kilometres (about 1,400 miles) over an area of roughly 344,400 square kilometres.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Made up of over 2,900 individual reefs and around 900 islands, built by billions of tiny coral polyps.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland in north-eastern Australia.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Selected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981 for its natural significance.

media.alt: Part of the Great Barrier Reef off the Queensland coast of Australia seen from orbit, showing turquoise reef structures against deep blue ocean.
media.attribution: NASA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the largest of the Egyptian pyramids and the centrepiece of the Giza pyramid complex near Cairo, Egypt. Built around 2600 BC as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu, it is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one to survive largely intact.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Constructed around 2600 BC as the tomb of the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu (Cheops).

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Originally about 146.6 metres (481 feet) tall; erosion of its outer casing has lowered it to roughly 138.5 metres.

facts.label: Record
facts.value: Was the tallest human-made structure in the world for more than 3,700 years.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Memphis and its Necropolis — the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur', inscribed in 1979.

media.alt: The Great Pyramid of Giza, a massive stepped limestone pyramid, under a clear sky in Giza, Egypt.
media.attribution: Photographer dedicated the work to the public domain under CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — The Great Pyramid of Giza (53242503167).jpg

summary.text: Petra is an ancient city and archaeological site in southern Jordan, famous for its rock-cut architecture and sophisticated water-management systems. Settled and developed by the Nabataeans, it became the capital of their kingdom and a major hub on the incense trade routes, and is often called the 'Rose City' for the colour of its sandstone.

facts.label: Founders
facts.value: Developed by the Nabataeans, a nomadic Arab people who settled the area from around the 4th century BC and made it their capital.

facts.label: Rock-cut architecture
facts.value: Its monuments, such as Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), were carved directly into coloured sandstone cliffs.

facts.label: Rediscovery
facts.value: Largely unknown to the Western world until 1812, when the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 as a cultural site.

media.alt: Al-Khazneh, the Treasury of Petra, an ornate classical facade carved into a rose-coloured sandstone cliff in Jordan.
media.attribution: Photographer, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Al-Khazneh (The Treasury), Petra, Jordan.jpg

summary.text: Rome is the capital city of Italy and of the Lazio region, set on the River Tiber in the central part of the Italian Peninsula. With a history spanning more than two and a half thousand years, it was the capital of the Roman Kingdom, Republic, and Empire, and is often called the 'Eternal City'.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: The capital of Italy and the country's most populous city.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Lies on the River Tiber in the Lazio region of central Italy.

facts.label: Ancient history
facts.value: Served in turn as the capital of the Roman Kingdom, the Roman Republic, and the Roman Empire.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The historic centre of Rome was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980.

media.alt: The Baroque Trevi Fountain in Rome, with sculpted figures and basins of water in front of a palace facade.
media.attribution: Diliff, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Trevi Fountain, Rome, Italy 2 - May 2007.jpg

summary.text: The Colosseum is a large oval amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, Italy. Built of travertine limestone, tuff, and brick-faced concrete, it was the largest amphitheatre of the Roman world and was used for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Construction began under the emperor Vespasian around AD 70-72 and was completed under Titus in AD 80.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: Estimated to have held tens of thousands of spectators for gladiatorial games and public events.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: The largest amphitheatre ever built, measuring roughly 189 by 156 metres at its outer base.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Historic Centre of Rome.

media.alt: The Colosseum in Rome, a large oval stone amphitheatre with tiers of arches, seen under a clear sky.
media.attribution: FeaturedPics, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

summary.text: Venice is a city in north-eastern Italy, built on a group of small islands in the Venetian Lagoon of the Adriatic Sea. Its buildings are linked by canals and bridges rather than roads, and for centuries it was the centre of a powerful maritime republic.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Built across more than a hundred small islands in the Venetian Lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea.

facts.label: Canals
facts.value: Lacks conventional roads in its historic core; movement is by canals, footbridges, and on foot.

facts.label: History
facts.value: Was the heart of the Republic of Venice, a major maritime and trading power for much of the medieval and early modern period.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Venice and its Lagoon were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

media.alt: Aerial view of Venice, its islands and canals set in the surrounding lagoon.
media.attribution: kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Santorini, officially Thira, is a Greek island in the southern Aegean Sea, the largest of a small circular archipelago that is the remnant of a volcanic caldera. A massive eruption in the Late Bronze Age shaped its dramatic cliffs, and whitewashed towns now perch along the caldera rim.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in the southern Aegean Sea, part of the Cyclades group of Greek islands.

facts.label: Volcanic origin
facts.value: The island is the remnant of a volcanic caldera, formed by repeated eruptions including a major Late Bronze Age event.

facts.label: Minoan eruption
facts.value: The Minoan (Theran) eruption devastated the island's Bronze Age settlement at Akrotiri and is among the largest volcanic events in recorded history.

media.alt: Satellite view of Santorini, Greece, showing the ring-shaped island surrounding its flooded volcanic caldera in the Aegean Sea.
media.attribution: NASA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Acropolis of Athens is an ancient citadel on a rocky outcrop above the city of Athens, Greece. It contains the remains of several buildings of great architectural and historical significance, the most famous being the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to the goddess Athena.

facts.label: Parthenon
facts.value: Its best-known monument is the Parthenon, a temple to Athena built in the 5th century BC.

facts.label: Golden Age
facts.value: Most of the major surviving buildings were constructed under the statesman Pericles during the 5th century BC.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Stands on a flat-topped rock rising about 150 metres above sea level in the centre of Athens.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

media.alt: The Acropolis of Athens on its rocky hill, lit up against the night sky.
media.attribution: Giles Laurent, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — 1029 Acropolis of Athens in Greece at night Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg

summary.text: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England. It consists of a ring of standing stones, each several metres high, and is one of the most famous prehistoric structures in the world.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: Built in several phases, with the stone settings erected between roughly 3000 and 2000 BC.

facts.label: Stones
facts.value: Comprises large sarsen stones and smaller bluestones, some transported from a considerable distance.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, southern England.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites', inscribed in 1986.

sources.name: UNESCO — Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites

media.alt: The standing stones of Stonehenge forming a ring on open grassland under a cloudy sky in Wiltshire, England.
media.attribution: garethwiscombe, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

summary.text: Iceland is a Nordic island country in the North Atlantic Ocean, lying on the boundary between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Shaped by intense volcanic and geothermal activity, it features glaciers, hot springs, geysers, and lava fields, and its capital is Reykjavik.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: Reykjavik, which is also the country's largest city.

facts.label: Geology
facts.value: Sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, making it highly volcanic and geothermally active.

facts.label: Aurora
facts.value: Its high-latitude position makes it a notable location for viewing the aurora borealis (northern lights) during dark winter months.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: Among the most sparsely populated countries in Europe, with roughly 390,000 inhabitants.

media.alt: Kirkjufell, a steep cone-shaped mountain on Iceland's Snæfellsnes peninsula.
media.attribution: Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Sahara is a desert spanning much of North Africa and is the largest hot desert in the world. Covering an area comparable to that of the United States or China, it stretches across numerous countries from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Covers about 9.2 million square kilometres, making it the largest hot desert on Earth.

facts.label: Extent
facts.value: Stretches across North Africa from the Atlantic Ocean in the west to the Red Sea in the east.

facts.label: Landscape
facts.value: Includes vast sand seas (ergs), stony plateaus, gravel plains, and mountain ranges, not only dunes.

media.alt: View of the Sahara desert from space, showing tan and orange sands across North Africa.
media.attribution: Project Apollo Archive (NASA), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Serengeti is a geographical region in East Africa, spanning northern Tanzania and extending into south-western Kenya. It is famous for its vast savanna plains and for the annual migration of enormous herds of wildebeest and zebra.

facts.label: Great Migration
facts.value: Hosts one of the largest terrestrial mammal migrations on Earth, as wildebeest and zebra move in search of grazing and water.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies mostly in northern Tanzania, reaching into south-western Kenya.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Serengeti National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981.

media.alt: Wide grassy plains of Serengeti National Park dotted with acacia trees.
media.attribution: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Victoria Falls is a waterfall on the Zambezi River at the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe in southern Africa. Known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the Smoke that Thunders', it is one of the largest waterfalls in the world by the combined width and height of its sheet of falling water.

facts.label: River
facts.value: Formed where the Zambezi River plunges into a series of gorges along the Zambia-Zimbabwe border.

facts.label: Dimensions
facts.value: Roughly 1,708 metres wide and over 100 metres high, producing an enormous curtain of water.

facts.label: Local name
facts.value: Known indigenously as Mosi-oa-Tunya, meaning 'the Smoke that Thunders'.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1989 as Mosi-oa-Tunya / Victoria Falls.

media.alt: Water plunging over the cliff of Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
media.attribution: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Cataratas Victoria, Zambia-Zimbabue, 2018-07-27, DD 04.jpg

summary.text: Table Mountain is a flat-topped mountain overlooking the city of Cape Town in South Africa. Its distinctive level plateau, often covered by a cap of cloud nicknamed the 'tablecloth', makes it a prominent landmark and a focus of the surrounding national park.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: Noted for its flat, roughly level summit plateau around three kilometres from side to side.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Overlooks Cape Town and Table Bay on the south-western coast of South Africa.

facts.label: National park
facts.value: Protected within Table Mountain National Park, which conserves part of the Cape Floristic Region's rich biodiversity.

media.alt: The flat-topped summit of Table Mountain rising above Cape Town, South Africa.
media.attribution: Danie van der Merwe, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Mount Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in Tanzania and the highest mountain in Africa. Rising freestanding from the surrounding plains, it has three volcanic cones and its highest peak, Uhuru, reaches well above the snow line despite lying near the equator.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: Its highest point, Uhuru Peak, rises to about 5,895 metres (19,341 feet) above sea level.

facts.label: Highest in Africa
facts.value: The tallest mountain on the African continent and the highest freestanding mountain in the world.

facts.label: Volcano
facts.value: A dormant stratovolcano made up of three cones: Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Kilimanjaro National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

media.alt: Mount Kilimanjaro rising above the plains of Amboseli.
media.attribution: Sergey Pesterev, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Marrakesh is a major city in the central part of Morocco, near the foothills of the Atlas Mountains. Founded in the 11th century, its walled old city (medina) is known for its souks, palaces, gardens, and the large square of Jemaa el-Fnaa.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: Established in the 11th century and historically an important imperial city of Morocco.

facts.label: Medina
facts.value: Its historic walled medina is a dense network of souks, mosques, and palaces centred on the Jemaa el-Fnaa square.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Lies on a plain near the foothills of the snow-capped Atlas Mountains in central Morocco.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Medina of Marrakesh was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985.

media.alt: Jemaa el-Fnaa, the large central square of Marrakesh, Morocco.
media.attribution: Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Jamaa El Fna, Marrakesh, Morocco, 20250124 1804 7017.jpg

summary.text: Istanbul is the largest city in Turkey, straddling the Bosphorus strait that separates Europe from Asia. Formerly known as Byzantium and then Constantinople, it served as the capital of the Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman empires.

facts.label: Two continents
facts.value: Spans the Bosphorus strait, with districts on both the European and Asian sides.

facts.label: Former names
facts.value: Known in antiquity as Byzantium and later as Constantinople before its present name.

facts.label: Imperial capital
facts.value: Served as the capital of the Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman empires across many centuries.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Historic Areas of Istanbul were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985.

media.alt: Panorama of Istanbul showing the historical peninsula beside the modern city skyline.
media.attribution: Hunanuk, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Historical peninsula and modern skyline of Istanbul.jpg

summary.text: Hagia Sophia is a large former church and mosque in Istanbul, Turkey. Built in the 6th century as the cathedral of Constantinople, it was for nearly a thousand years the world's largest interior space and a masterpiece of Byzantine architecture, celebrated for its vast central dome.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Completed in AD 537 under the Byzantine emperor Justinian I.

facts.label: Dome
facts.value: Famous for its enormous central dome, a landmark achievement of Byzantine engineering.

facts.label: Changing uses
facts.value: Served as a cathedral, then a mosque, later a museum, and again a mosque over its long history.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Historic Areas of Istanbul.

media.alt: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, with its large central dome and surrounding minarets.
media.attribution: Adli Wahid, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the south bank of the Yamuna River in Agra, India. It was commissioned in the 17th century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and is widely regarded as a jewel of Mughal architecture.

facts.label: Commissioned
facts.value: Built on the orders of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Construction began around 1632 and the mausoleum was largely completed by about 1648.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Faced in white marble inlaid with precious and semi-precious stones.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983.

media.alt: The white marble Taj Mahal mausoleum with its central dome and four minarets, reflected in the long watercourse of its garden in Agra, India.
media.attribution: Yann Forget, edited by Jim Carter, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

summary.text: Varanasi, also known as Benares or Kashi, is a city on the banks of the River Ganges in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a major spiritual centre, famous for its riverside steps known as ghats.

facts.label: River
facts.value: Sits on the banks of the River Ganges in northern India.

facts.label: Antiquity
facts.value: Regarded as one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

facts.label: Ghats
facts.value: Known for its many ghats, riverfront steps leading down to the Ganges used for bathing and rituals.

media.alt: The ghats of Varanasi on the bank of the Ganges, where a cremation ceremony is taking place.
media.attribution: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Varanasi, India, Ghats, Cremation ceremony in progress.jpg

summary.text: Angkor Wat is a vast temple complex in northern Cambodia, originally built in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple dedicated to the god Vishnu and later gradually transformed into a Buddhist site. It is the largest religious monument in the world by land area and a symbol of Cambodia.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Constructed in the first half of the 12th century under the Khmer king Suryavarman II.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: The largest religious structure in the world by land area.

facts.label: Shifting faith
facts.value: Began as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu and was later converted to Buddhist use.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Angkor, inscribed in 1992.

media.alt: The main complex of Angkor Wat with its towers reflected in the water, photographed in late-afternoon light in Cambodia.
media.attribution: Bjorn Christian Torrissen, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

summary.text: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the historical northern borders of China. Constructed, rebuilt, and maintained over many centuries by successive dynasties, it was intended to protect Chinese states against raids and invasions from the north.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: Built as a line of fortifications to defend Chinese territory against incursions from the north.

facts.label: Long history
facts.value: Built and rebuilt across many dynasties; much of the best-known surviving wall dates from the Ming dynasty.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Archaeological surveys put the total length of all its branches at well over 20,000 kilometres.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

media.alt: A section of the Great Wall of China winding over green ridgelines at Jinshanling, with watchtowers along the stone rampart.
media.attribution: Severin.stalder, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling-edit.jpg

summary.text: The Forbidden City is a vast palace complex in the centre of Beijing, China. It served as the home of emperors and the ceremonial and political centre of Chinese government for roughly five centuries, from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: The imperial palace and seat of government for Ming and Qing dynasty emperors.

facts.label: Built
facts.value: Constructed in the early 15th century, between about 1406 and 1420.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Covers a large walled area containing hundreds of surviving buildings and many rooms.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987 as the Imperial Palace of the Ming and Qing Dynasties.

sources.name: UNESCO — Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties

media.alt: The rooftops of the Forbidden City in Beijing seen from Coal Hill (Jingshan).
media.attribution: Pixelflake, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — The Forbidden City - View from Coal Hill.jpg

summary.text: Bali is a province and island of Indonesia, lying at the western end of the Lesser Sunda Islands. Known for its volcanic mountains, terraced rice fields, beaches, and distinctive Hindu culture, it is one of Indonesia's most visited regions.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: An Indonesian island at the western end of the Lesser Sunda Islands, east of Java.

facts.label: Landscape
facts.value: Features volcanic peaks and extensive terraced rice paddies irrigated by a traditional system.

facts.label: Culture
facts.value: The majority of its population practises Balinese Hinduism, distinct within mostly Muslim Indonesia.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Its subak irrigation landscape was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012.

summary.text: The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre on the harbour in Sydney, Australia. Designed by the Danish architect Jorn Utzon, its series of shell-like roofs make it one of the most recognisable buildings of the 20th century.

facts.label: Architect
facts.value: Designed by the Danish architect Jorn Utzon, who won an international design competition for it.

facts.label: Opened
facts.value: Formally opened in 1973 after a long and complex construction.

facts.label: Design
facts.value: Noted for its distinctive series of precast concrete 'shells' forming the roofs.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2007.

media.alt: The Sydney Opera House at dusk, its white sail-shaped shells lit against the darkening sky beside Sydney Harbour.

summary.text: Uluru, also known as Ayers Rock, is a large sandstone rock formation in the southern part of the Northern Territory in central Australia. It is sacred to the Anangu, the Aboriginal people of the area, and is one of Australia's most recognisable natural landmarks.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Rises about 348 metres above the surrounding plain, with much more of its bulk below ground.

facts.label: Cultural significance
facts.value: Sacred to the Anangu, the Aboriginal traditional owners of the land.

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: Its sandstone appears to glow red at sunrise and sunset due to the way light strikes the surface.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

media.alt: Uluru, a large red sandstone monolith rising from the flat central Australian landscape.
media.attribution: Ek2030372672, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Christ the Redeemer is a large Art Deco statue of Jesus Christ overlooking the city of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Standing atop the Corcovado mountain with its arms outstretched, it is one of the most recognisable monuments in South America.

facts.label: Completed
facts.value: Built between 1922 and 1931 atop the Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: The statue stands about 30 metres tall, with an arm span of roughly 28 metres, atop a pedestal.

facts.label: Style
facts.value: Built in reinforced concrete faced with soapstone in an Art Deco style.

media.alt: The Christ the Redeemer statue standing with outstretched arms on the Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
media.attribution: Arne Museler / www.arne-mueseler.com, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 DE)

summary.text: The Amazon Rainforest is a vast tropical rainforest covering much of the Amazon basin in South America. It is the largest rainforest on Earth, spanning several countries, and is home to an extraordinary diversity of plant and animal life.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: The largest tropical rainforest in the world, covering roughly 5.5 million square kilometres.

facts.label: Extent
facts.value: Spans parts of several South American countries, with the majority lying within Brazil.

facts.label: Biodiversity
facts.value: Holds one of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet, with millions of species.

media.alt: Dense tropical rainforest vegetation in the Amazon.
media.attribution: CIAT, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Galapagos Islands are a volcanic archipelago in the Pacific Ocean, part of Ecuador and lying on the equator about a thousand kilometres from the mainland. Their isolated ecosystems host many species found nowhere else and famously influenced Charles Darwin's thinking on evolution.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: A volcanic archipelago belonging to Ecuador, straddling the equator in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

facts.label: Endemic wildlife
facts.value: Home to many endemic species, including giant tortoises and marine iguanas.

facts.label: Darwin
facts.value: The wildlife Charles Darwin observed here during the 1835 voyage of HMS Beagle helped shape his theory of natural selection.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Among the first sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, in 1978.

media.alt: A Galápagos sea lion at Punta Pitt on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos.
media.attribution: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Chichen Itza is a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya civilization on the Yucatan Peninsula of present-day Mexico. One of the largest Maya cities, it is dominated by the stepped pyramid known as El Castillo, dedicated to the feathered-serpent deity Kukulcan.

facts.label: Builders
facts.value: A major city of the Maya civilization, flourishing from around the late Classic into the early Postclassic period.

facts.label: El Castillo
facts.value: Its best-known structure is the step pyramid El Castillo (the Temple of Kukulcan).

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in the state of Yucatan in south-eastern Mexico.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1988.

media.alt: Stone ruins at the Maya archaeological site of Chichen Itza in Yucatán, Mexico.
media.attribution: Daniel Schwen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Pompeii was an ancient Roman city near modern Naples in the Campania region of Italy. It was buried under volcanic ash and pumice in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, which preserved much of the city and provides a detailed record of life in the Roman world.

facts.label: Destroyed
facts.value: Buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, which covered the city in ash and pumice.

facts.label: Preservation
facts.value: The volcanic deposits preserved buildings, frescoes, and everyday objects in remarkable detail.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lay near the Bay of Naples in the Campania region of southern Italy.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site covering the archaeological areas of Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Torre Annunziata, inscribed in 1997.

sources.name: UNESCO — Archaeological Areas of Pompeii, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata

media.alt: Aerial view of the ruins of Pompeii with Mount Vesuvius in the background, seen from the southeast.
media.attribution: Carsten Steger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Lalibela is a town in Ethiopia's Amhara Region, known for its rock-cut monolithic churches. The wider town is regarded as an important site for the history of Ethiopian civilization, and for some Christians it is among the country's holiest cities and a place of pilgrimage.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in the Lasta district and North Wollo Zone of the Amhara Region, Ethiopia.

facts.label: Rock-cut churches
facts.value: Famous for monolithic churches cut from the rock, designed in contrast to the earlier monolithic churches in Ethiopia.

facts.label: Pilgrimage
facts.value: To some Christians it is one of Ethiopia's holiest cities and a center of pilgrimage.

media.alt: Exterior view of the Church of Saint George at Lalibela, Ethiopia.
media.attribution: Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Okavango Delta is a large inland delta in Botswana. It forms where the Okavango River reaches a tectonic trough in the endorheic basin of the Kalahari Desert.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in Botswana, in the central part of the Kalahari Desert's endorheic basin.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: Sits at an elevation of about 930 to 1,000 metres (3,050 to 3,280 feet).

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: Created where the Okavango River meets a tectonic trough, rather than flowing on to the sea.

media.alt: Landscape photograph of the Okavango Delta in Botswana.
media.attribution: Joachim Huber, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Namib is a coastal desert running along the Atlantic coast of southern Africa, through Angola, Namibia and northwest South Africa. It is extremely dry and may be the oldest desert in the world.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: By the broadest definition it stretches for more than 2,000 kilometres (1,200 miles) along the Atlantic coast.

facts.label: Rainfall
facts.value: Annual precipitation ranges from about 2 millimetres in the driest regions to 200 millimetres at the escarpment.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Arid or semi-arid conditions have lasted roughly 55 to 80 million years, so it may be the world's oldest desert.

media.alt: Satellite image of the Namib Desert along the southwestern coast of Africa, taken by NASA's MODIS instrument.
media.attribution: Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Ngorongoro Crater is a large volcanic caldera that gives its name to the Ngorongoro Conservation Area in northeastern Tanzania. The protected area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and borders Serengeti National Park.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies about 180 km (110 mi) west of Arusha City, in the Crater Highlands of northeastern Tanzania.

facts.label: Neighbouring parks
facts.value: The western portion of the conservation area abuts Serengeti National Park.

facts.label: Olduvai Gorge
facts.value: The conservation area contains Olduvai Gorge, one of the most important paleoanthropological sites in the world.

media.alt: View of the Ngorongoro Crater landscape in Tanzania.
media.attribution: Grahampurse, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Stone Town, also called Mji Mkongwe, is the old part of Zanzibar City in Tanzania. It was the capital of the Sultanate of Zanzibar and a centre of the 19th-century spice trade.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Sits on the western coast of Unguja, the main island of the Zanzibar Archipelago.

facts.label: Local name
facts.value: Known as Mji Mkongwe; the newer part of the city is called Ng'ambo, Swahili for 'the other side'.

facts.label: Trade history
facts.value: In the 19th century it was a flourishing centre of both the spice trade and the Indian Ocean slave trade.

media.alt: The Sultan's Palace in Stone Town, Zanzibar.
media.attribution: Mbz1 (assumed author), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Timbuktu is a city in Mali, about 20 kilometres north of the Niger River. It is the capital of the Tombouctou Region, one of Mali's 19 administrative regions.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Situated 20 kilometres north of the Niger River in Mali.

facts.label: Regional capital
facts.value: Capital of the Tombouctou Region, one of the 19 administrative regions of Mali.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: Around 84,000 people in the 2023 census.

media.alt: Donkeys photographed in Timbuktu, Mali.
media.attribution: Emilio Labrador (Flickr), CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, lying off the southeastern coast of Africa. It includes the main island and many smaller islands around it, and its capital and largest city is Antananarivo.

facts.label: Island rank
facts.value: The world's fourth-largest island.

facts.label: Country rank
facts.value: The second-largest island country and the 46th-largest country overall.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: Antananarivo is both the capital and the largest city.

summary.text: New York City is the most populous city in the United States, set at the southern tip of New York State on New York Harbor. It is made up of five boroughs and is a major centre of finance, culture, media and international diplomacy, and the home of the United Nations headquarters.

facts.label: Boroughs
facts.value: Five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island, each coextensive with its own county.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: An estimated 8,586,038 people as of 2026, spread over 300.46 square miles (778.2 km²).

facts.label: Early history
facts.value: Dutch colonists founded a settlement on Manhattan Island that was named New Amsterdam in 1626 and chartered as a city in 1653. English control began in 1664, and the name New York was permanently adopted in 1674.

facts.label: Languages
facts.value: An estimated 800 languages are spoken in the city, making it the most linguistically diverse city in the world.

media.alt: The Empire State Building lit in green at sunset, rising above the Midtown Manhattan skyline as seen from the Top of the Rock observation deck.

summary.text: The Statue of Liberty is a colossal copper-clad sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was a gift from the people of France to the United States and has become an icon of freedom and a symbol of welcome to immigrants arriving by sea.

facts.label: Dedicated
facts.value: Dedicated on October 28, 1886, in a ceremony presided over by President Grover Cleveland.

facts.label: Designers
facts.value: Designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel.

facts.label: The tablet
facts.value: The tablet in her left hand is inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, the date of the Declaration of Independence in Roman numerals.

facts.label: Stewardship
facts.value: Maintained by the National Park Service since 1933 as part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument. Public access to the torch has been barred since 1916.

summary.text: The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge across the one-mile-wide strait that connects San Francisco Bay with the Pacific Ocean. It links San Francisco to Marin County and is one of the most recognized symbols of San Francisco and California.

facts.label: Opened
facts.value: Opened to the public on May 27, 1937.

facts.label: Main span
facts.value: The main span is 4,200 feet (1,280 m) and the total height is 746 feet (227 m).

facts.label: Record at opening
facts.value: In 1937 it was both the longest and the tallest suspension bridge in the world.

facts.label: Engineering
facts.value: Joseph Strauss was chief engineer, with Leon Moisseiff, Irving Morrow and Charles Ellis making significant contributions to the design.

media.alt: The Golden Gate Bridge's orange-red towers and suspension cables stretching across the strait, seen from Battery East in San Francisco.

summary.text: Yellowstone is a national park in the western United States, lying mainly in northwest Wyoming with small parts in Montana and Idaho. It is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, and is widely regarded as the first national park in the world.

facts.label: Established
facts.value: Created by an act of Congress signed by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Spans 3,468.4 square miles (8,983 km²).

facts.label: Geothermal features
facts.value: Well over half of the world's geysers and hydrothermal features are found here, fueled by ongoing volcanism of the Yellowstone Caldera, which has erupted twice with tremendous force in the last two million years.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.

media.alt: The Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River plunging into the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, framed by steep canyon walls.

summary.text: Yosemite is a national park in California's Sierra Nevada, managed by the National Park Service. It is internationally recognized for its granite cliffs, waterfalls, giant sequoia groves, meadows and rich biological diversity.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Covers 1,187 square miles (3,070 km²) across four counties.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Designated a World Heritage Site in 1984.

facts.label: Wilderness
facts.value: Almost 95 percent of the park is designated wilderness, and it is one of the largest and least fragmented habitat blocks in the Sierra Nevada.

media.alt: Half Dome's granite face rising above the forested eastern Yosemite Valley, viewed from Glacier Point.

summary.text: Niagara Falls is a group of three waterfalls at the southern end of Niagara Gorge, on the border between Ontario in Canada and New York in the United States. Fed by the Niagara River, which drains Lake Erie into Lake Ontario, the falls have the highest flow rate of any waterfall in North America.

facts.label: Three falls
facts.value: Horseshoe Falls (also called the Canadian Falls) is the largest; the smaller American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls lie within the United States.

facts.label: Flow
facts.value: During peak daytime tourist hours, more than 168,000 cubic metres of water goes over the crest every minute.

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: Formed when glaciers receded at the end of the Wisconsin glaciation, the last ice age, and water from the newly formed Great Lakes carved a path through the Niagara Escarpment.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies 27 kilometres (17 miles) northwest of Buffalo, New York, and 69 kilometres (43 miles) southeast of Toronto.

media.alt: The American, Bridal Veil and Horseshoe Falls seen together from the Canadian side under a partly cloudy sky.
media.attribution: Saffron Blaze, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Banff National Park lies in the Rocky Mountains of Alberta, Canada, and is the country's first national park. Its mountainous terrain includes glaciers and ice fields, dense coniferous forest and alpine landscapes.

facts.label: Established
facts.value: Founded in 1885 as Rocky Mountains Park, Canada's first national park.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Encompasses 6,641 square kilometres (2,564 sq mi) of mountainous terrain.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Located 110–180 kilometres (68–112 miles) west of Calgary, with the town of Banff in the Bow River valley as its main commercial centre.

facts.label: Neighbours
facts.value: Bordered by Jasper National Park to the north, and by Yoho and Kootenay National Parks to the west in British Columbia.

media.alt: Moraine Lake in the Valley of the Ten Peaks, with a ring of snow-dusted mountains reflected in the still water and conifer forest along the shore.
media.attribution: Gorgo (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico and the most populous city in North America. It lies in the Valley of Mexico on the high central plateau, and grew from the Mexica city of Tenochtitlan, which was built on islands in Lake Texcoco.

facts.label: Altitude
facts.value: Sits at about 2,240 metres (7,350 feet) above sea level in the Valley of Mexico.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: The 2020 census counted 9,209,944 people in the city proper and 21,804,515 in Greater Mexico City.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: Began as Tenochtitlan, a Mexica city built around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco.

facts.label: Administration
facts.value: Divided into 16 boroughs, known as alcaldías.

media.alt: Aerial photograph looking out over the dense streets and buildings of Mexico City.
media.attribution: Gobierno CDMX, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Teotihuacan is an ancient Mesoamerican city in the Valley of Mexico, about 40 kilometres northeast of modern Mexico City. It is known for the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Avenue of the Dead, and it predates the Aztec Empire by many centuries.

facts.label: Peak
facts.value: At its height, in the first half of the first millennium CE, it was the largest city in the Americas, with a population likely around 100,000.

facts.label: Founding
facts.value: The city is thought to have been established around 100 BCE, with major monuments under construction until about 250 CE.

facts.label: Decline
facts.value: Its major monuments were sacked and systematically burned around 550 CE.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The site covers 83 square kilometres and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

media.alt: The stepped Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan, Mexico, seen from a path across the site.
media.attribution: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Iguazu Falls are a system of waterfalls on the Iguazu River, on the border between the Argentine province of Misiones and the Brazilian state of Paraná. Together they form the largest waterfall system in the world, with most of the falls on the Argentine side.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: On the Iguazu River, where it forms the border between Argentina and Brazil.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Iguazú comes from Guarani or Tupi words meaning 'water' and 'big'.

facts.label: European record
facts.value: The first European to record the falls was the Spanish conquistador Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, in 1541.

facts.label: Protection
facts.value: Protected within national parks in Argentina and Brazil, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984 and 1986 respectively.

media.alt: Iguazu Falls seen from the Brazilian side, with many cascades pouring into the river gorge.

summary.text: Torres del Paine National Park protects mountains, glaciers, lakes and rivers in southern Chilean Patagonia. Its centrepiece is the Cordillera del Paine, a mountain group that rises from the transition between subpolar forest and Patagonian steppe.

sources.name: Wikipedia — Torres del Paine National Park

facts.label: Established
facts.value: Created as a national park in 1959.

sources.name: Wikipedia — Torres del Paine National Park

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Measured approximately 181,414 hectares (700 square miles) in 2013.

sources.name: Wikipedia — Torres del Paine National Park

facts.label: The Towers
facts.value: Three granite peaks (Torre d'Agostini, Torre Central and Torre Monzino) rise about 2,500 metres (8,200 feet) above sea level.

sources.name: Wikipedia — Torres del Paine National Park

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Paine means 'blue' in the Tehuelche (Aonikenk) language.

sources.name: Wikipedia — Torres del Paine National Park

summary.text: Easter Island is a special territory of Chile in the southeastern Pacific Ocean, at the southeastern tip of the Polynesian Triangle. It is best known for its nearly 1,000 surviving moai, monumental statues carved by the early Rapa Nui people.

facts.label: Remoteness
facts.value: One of the world's most remote inhabited islands; the nearest continental point, in central Chile, is 3,512 kilometres away.

facts.label: Settlement
facts.value: Experts differ on when Polynesians arrived: evidence points to around 800 CE, while a 2007 study suggested closer to 1200.

facts.label: Chilean annexation
facts.value: Chile annexed the island in 1888.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995, with much of the island protected within Rapa Nui National Park.

media.alt: An ahu, a stone ceremonial platform, on Easter Island, with the town of Hanga Roa in the background.

summary.text: Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, lying in southwestern Bolivia near the crest of the Andes. It covers roughly 10,500 square kilometres of high-altitude plain.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Approximately 10,582 square kilometres (4,086 square miles).

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: Sits at 3,656 metres (11,995 feet) above sea level.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: In Daniel Campos Province, Potosí Department, southwestern Bolivia.

media.alt: Small mounds of harvested salt on the flat white surface of the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia.

summary.text: Tokyo is the capital of Japan and the country's most populous city. Its metropolitan area, which reaches into several neighbouring prefectures, is one of the largest urban regions on Earth.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Officially the Tokyo Metropolis, it is the capital and most populous city of Japan.

facts.label: City population
facts.value: The city proper had a population of over 14 million as of 2023.

facts.label: Greater Tokyo Area
facts.value: Including parts of six neighbouring prefectures, it is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.

summary.text: Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, and the largest city in all of Korea. Together with Gyeonggi Province and Incheon it forms a metropolitan area that holds more than half of the country's people.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Officially Seoul Special Metropolitan City, it is the capital and largest city of South Korea.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 9.6 million residents as of 2024. The figure peaked at over 10 million and has gradually declined since 2014.

facts.label: Metropolitan area
facts.value: The Seoul Metropolitan Area, covering Seoul, Gyeonggi Province and Incheon, was the world's sixth largest metropolitan economy in 2022 and hosts more than half of South Korea's population.

media.alt: Junghwajeon, a traditional Korean palace hall at Deoksugung in central Seoul, photographed in daylight.

summary.text: Singapore is an island country and city-state in Southeast Asia, sitting just off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. It is made up of one main island and dozens of smaller islets.

facts.label: Official name
facts.value: The Republic of Singapore, an island country and city-state in Southeast Asia.

facts.label: Territory
facts.value: A main island, over 60 satellite islands and islets, and one outlying islet.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: About one degree of latitude north of the equator, bordering the Strait of Malacca to the west, the Singapore Strait to the south, and the Straits of Johor to the north.

summary.text: Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level. It rises in the Mahalangur Himal of the Himalayas, and its summit lies on the border between China and Nepal.

facts.label: Rank
facts.value: The highest mountain on Earth above sea level.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: 8,848.86 metres, as measured in 2020 by a joint survey of Nepalese and Chinese authorities.

facts.label: Range
facts.value: Part of the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas.

facts.label: Border
facts.value: Its summit marks part of the China–Nepal border.
