summary.text: Hạ Long Bay is a bay in northeastern Vietnam, administered by the city of Quảng Ninh. It is known for thousands of limestone karsts and islets, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Northeastern Vietnam, administered by the city of Quảng Ninh.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Hạ Long means "descending dragon".

facts.label: Landscape
facts.value: Thousands of limestone karsts and islets of various shapes and sizes.

facts.label: Wider area
facts.value: It is part of a larger area that includes Bai Tu Long Bay to the northeast and Cát Bà Island to the southwest, which share similar geological and climatic characteristics.

media.alt: Panoramic view of Ha Long Bay from Titov Island, with limestone islets rising from the water and boats below.
media.attribution: Taewangkorea, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Ha Long Bay in 2019.jpg

summary.text: Borobudur is a Mahayana Buddhist temple from the 9th century in Central Java, Indonesia. It stands in Magelang Regency, near the town of Muntilan and northwest of Yogyakarta.

facts.label: Period
facts.value: A 9th-century temple.

facts.label: Tradition
facts.value: A Mahayana Buddhist temple, also transcribed Barabudur.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Magelang Regency in Central Java, Indonesia, near Muntilan and northwest of the city of Yogyakarta.

media.alt: Buddhist monks walking around Borobudur temple in a pradaksina, the ritual circumambulation of the monument.
media.attribution: Heri nugroho, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Bagan is a medieval city and UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Mandalay Region of Myanmar. It was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, and thousands of Buddhist temples and pagodas were raised on its plains.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: From the 9th to 13th centuries it was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, the first kingdom to unify the regions that later made up Myanmar.

facts.label: Temples built
facts.value: At the kingdom's height, between the 11th and 13th centuries, more than 10,000 Buddhist temples, pagodas and monasteries were constructed on the Bagan plains.

facts.label: Temples surviving
facts.value: The remains of over 2,300 temples and pagodas survive.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The Mandalay Region of Myanmar.

media.alt: View over the plain of Bagan in Myanmar, with temples and pagodas scattered across the landscape.
media.attribution: Corto Maltese 1999, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Potala Palace is a hilltop palace complex in Lhasa, in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. It served as the winter palace and residence of the Dalai Lamas and is now a museum. Its name comes from Mount Potalaka, a legendary Buddhist abode of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.

facts.label: Residence
facts.value: From 1649 until 1959 it served as the residence of the Dalai Lamas.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: Work on the present structure began in 1645 at the order of the 5th Dalai Lama, on the site of an earlier palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: It rises 13 stories at an altitude of about 3,700 metres and contains more than 1,000 rooms and some 200,000 statues.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994.

media.alt: The Potala Palace in Lhasa, Tibet, seen from the foot of Chagpo Ri hill.
media.attribution: Ondřej Žváček, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Terracotta Army is a collection of clay sculptures depicting the soldiers of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China. The figures were buried with him around 210 to 209 BCE to protect him in the afterlife. They lie near Xi'an in Shaanxi Province.

facts.label: Discovery
facts.value: Found on 29 March 1974 by farmers digging a well east of the emperor's tomb mound.

facts.label: Size of the army
facts.value: Estimates from 2007 put the three pits at more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses.

facts.label: Figures
facts.value: The warriors are life-sized, typically 1.75 to about 2 metres tall, with officers usually taller, and their faces differ from figure to figure.

facts.label: Painted figures
facts.value: The figures were originally painted, but much of the colour coating flakes off within minutes of exposure to Xi'an's dry air.

media.alt: Rows of life-sized terracotta warrior figures standing in an excavation pit at the Terracotta Army site near Xi'an, China.
media.attribution: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Wulingyuan is a scenic reserve in Hunan Province, China, known for thousands of tall sandstone pillars rising above forested valleys. The area also holds gorges, streams, waterfalls, caves, and a very high natural bridge. It shelters several vulnerable animal species.

facts.label: Sandstone pillars
facts.value: More than 3,000 quartzite sandstone pillars and peaks, many over 200 metres high.

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: The pillars formed during the Devonian period, 400 to 350 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and water erosion.

facts.label: Caves and bridge
facts.value: It has 40 caves and a natural bridge called Tianqiaoshengkong, meaning 'bridge across the sky'.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992.

media.alt: Panoramic view from Mount Tianzi of Wulingyuan, with tall sandstone pillars rising from forested valleys in Hunan, China.
media.attribution: chensiyuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, and the deepest lake in the world. It holds more fresh water by volume than any other lake and is among the oldest and clearest. Many of the plants and animals living there are found nowhere else.

facts.label: Maximum depth
facts.value: 1,642 metres (5,387 feet), the deepest lake in the world.

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 31,722 square kilometres, roughly 636 km long and 79 km wide.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: At an estimated 25 to 30 million years, it is the world's oldest lake.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: UNESCO declared Baikal a World Heritage Site in 1996.

media.alt: Satellite view of Lake Baikal in southern Siberia, a long crescent-shaped lake, captured by NASA's Terra/MODIS sensor.
media.attribution: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Sigiriya, also called Lion Rock, is an ancient rock fortress in central Sri Lanka near the town of Dambulla. A tall column of granite dominates the site, which holds the remains of a fifth-century royal city. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.label: The rock
facts.value: A massive granite column approximately 180 metres high.

facts.label: Royal capital
facts.value: King Kashyapa (477 to 495 CE) chose the site for his new capital and built his palace on top of the rock.

facts.label: Later use
facts.value: After the king's death the capital was abandoned, and the site was used as a Buddhist monastery until the 14th century.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 as the Ancient City of Sigiriya.

media.alt: The granite rock of Sigiriya rising above the surrounding plain in Sri Lanka.
media.attribution: Wrobell, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Kathmandu Valley is a bowl-shaped valley in the Himalayas of Nepal and the country's largest urban area. It sits at a crossroads of ancient South and East Asian civilizations and holds at least 130 important monuments. Several of them are Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage sites.

facts.label: World Heritage Sites
facts.value: The valley holds seven World Heritage Sites.

facts.label: Monuments
facts.value: It has at least 130 important monuments, including several Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage sites.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 5 million people live in the valley's urban agglomeration, the largest in Nepal.

facts.label: Name of Kathmandu
facts.value: The name comes from Kasthamandap, a wooden pavilion in Kathmandu Durbar Square built in 1596.

media.alt: Astronaut photograph from the International Space Station showing the Kathmandu metropolitan area, pale grey, ringed by green vegetated slopes.
media.attribution: ISS Expedition 25 crew, NASA Earth Observatory, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Bangkok, called Krung Thep Maha Nakhon in Thai, is the capital and largest city of Thailand. It lies in the Chao Phraya River delta and began as a small trading post in the Ayutthaya era. Today it is home to the Grand Palace and many Buddhist temples.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: The city covers 1,568.7 square kilometres in the Chao Phraya River delta of central Thailand.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: An estimated 9.1 million people in 2024, with over 17.4 million in the wider metropolitan region.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: It grew from a trading post in the 15th century and was founded as the capital on 21 April 1782 by Rama I.

media.alt: View of Bangkok's skyline and skyscrapers, photographed from the State Tower.
media.attribution: Ninara, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Paris is the capital and largest city of France, set on the Seine in the Île-de-France region. It is often called the City of Light, a nickname tied to its leading role in the Age of Enlightenment.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 2.04 million people live in the city proper (January 2026 estimate), within a metropolitan area of roughly 13.3 million (2023).

facts.label: Area
facts.value: The city covers about 105.4 square kilometres.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies on the Seine in the centre of the Île-de-France region.

facts.label: Nickname
facts.value: Known as the "City of Light", mainly because of its leading role in the Age of Enlightenment.

media.alt: The Eiffel Tower rising above the rooftops of Paris, seen from the Tour Saint-Jacques with the Seine and its bridges in view.
media.attribution: Yann Caradec, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — La Tour Eiffel vue de la Tour Saint-Jacques, Paris août 2014 (2).jpg

summary.text: London is the capital and largest city of England and the United Kingdom, standing on the River Thames in the southeast of England. Founded by the Romans as Londinium, it has been a major settlement for nearly 2,000 years.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 9.14 million people in 2025, with a wider metropolitan area of 15.4 million, the largest in Western Europe.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: The City of London was founded by the Romans as Londinium and has kept its medieval boundaries.

facts.label: River
facts.value: Stands on the Thames, at the head of a 50-mile (80 km) tidal estuary running down to the North Sea.

facts.label: Government
facts.value: The City of Westminster has been the site of the national government and parliament for centuries.

media.alt: The London skyline at sunset, with the River Thames, Tower Bridge and the financial district's towers seen from above.
media.attribution: Ilya Grigorik, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Sagrada Família is a Catholic basilica still under construction in the Eixample district of Barcelona, Spain. Designed by the architect Antoni Gaudí, it is the tallest church in the world.

facts.label: Architect
facts.value: Designed by the Spanish architect Antoni Gaudí.

facts.label: Consecration
facts.value: Pope Benedict XVI consecrated the church and proclaimed it a basilica on 7 November 2010.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: It is the tallest church in the world.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: In 2005, parts of the building were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site under "Works of Antoni Gaudí".

media.alt: Exterior of the Sagrada Família in Barcelona, showing the carved stone sculpture of its Passion Facade.
media.attribution: Reda Kerbush, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Exterior of the Sagrada Família.jpg

summary.text: The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain. It is among the best-known monuments of Islamic architecture and also holds notable examples of Spanish Renaissance architecture.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Granada, Spain.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: A palace and fortress complex.

facts.label: Rarity
facts.value: It is described as the only well-preserved palace from the medieval Islamic world.

media.alt: The Palace of Charles V within the Alhambra complex in Granada at dawn, seen from a viewpoint across the valley.
media.attribution: Jebulon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Dawn Charles V Palace Alhambra Granada Andalusia Spain.jpg

summary.text: The Palace of Versailles is a château and historic monument in the Yvelines department of France, southwest of Paris. It served as the principal residence of the French kings Louis XIV, Louis XV and Louis XVI.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: In Versailles, in the Yvelines department, southwest of Paris.

facts.label: Royal residence
facts.value: The principal residence of Louis XIV, Louis XV and Louis XVI.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: A château and historic monument.

media.alt: Aerial view of the Palace of Versailles and its formal gardens in France.
media.attribution: ToucanWings, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Versailles Palace (FRA) – Equestrian Olympic Venue.jpg

summary.text: Neuschwanstein Castle is a 19th-century historicist palace on a rugged hill in the Alpine foothills of southern Bavaria, Germany, near the Austrian border. It stands in the municipality of Schwangau, above the village of Hohenschwangau.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: In the Swabia region of Bavaria, in the municipality of Schwangau; the nearest larger town is Füssen.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: The castle stands above the narrow gorge of the Pöllat stream, east of the Alpsee and Schwansee lakes.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: According to Guinness World Records, at 65 metres it is the tallest castle in the world.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Since 2025 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "The Palaces of King Ludwig II of Bavaria".

media.alt: Neuschwanstein Castle perched on a wooded hill in the Bavarian Alps, photographed from the Marienbrücke.
media.attribution: Thomas Wolf (www.foto-tw.de), CC BY-SA 3.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Matterhorn is a near-symmetric pyramidal peak of the Pennine Alps on the border between Switzerland and Italy. At 4,478 metres, it is one of the highest summits in the Alps and has become an emblem of Switzerland.

facts.label: Summit elevation
facts.value: 4,478 metres (14,692 ft) above sea level.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: On the main watershed and border between Switzerland and Italy, in the Monte Rosa area of the Pennine Alps.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: A large, near-symmetric pyramidal peak.

facts.label: Nickname
facts.value: Sometimes called the "Mountain of Mountains".

media.alt: The pyramid-shaped Matterhorn seen from the Domhütte in Valais, with its rock faces and snow-streaked ridges.
media.attribution: Photo: chil (Camptocamp.org); derivative work: Zacharie Grossen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Geirangerfjord is a fjord in the Sunnmøre region of Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is a short branch of a larger fjord system, and the small village of Geiranger sits at its head where a river flows in.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: The fjord is about 15 kilometres long.

facts.label: Fjord system
facts.value: It branches off the Sunnylvsfjorden, which is itself a branch of the Storfjorden.

facts.label: Municipality
facts.value: The fjord lies entirely within Stranda Municipality.

facts.label: Village
facts.value: The village of Geiranger is at the end of the fjord, where the Geirangelva river empties into it.

media.alt: Geirangerfjord seen from above, a narrow blue fjord between steep green mountains with cloud shadows on the slopes.
media.attribution: Andreas Trepte, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Giant's Causeway is a stretch of coast in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, covered with about 40,000 interlocking basalt columns. The columns formed in an ancient volcanic fissure eruption during the Paleogene period.

facts.label: Columns
facts.value: The site has approximately 40,000 interlocking basalt columns.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: The columns resulted from a volcanic fissure eruption, part of the North Atlantic Igneous Province active during the Paleogene period.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: It lies on the north coast of County Antrim, about three miles northeast of Bushmills.

media.alt: Dark hexagonal basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway stepping down to the sea, with waves breaking on the rock.
media.attribution: code poet, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: The Cliffs of Moher are sea cliffs on the southwestern edge of the Burren region in County Clare, Ireland. They stretch for roughly 14 kilometres along the Atlantic coast, with O'Brien's Tower near their midpoint.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: The cliffs run for about 14 kilometres.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: They rise 120 metres at Hag's Head in the south and reach a maximum of 214 metres just north of O'Brien's Tower.

facts.label: O'Brien's Tower
facts.value: A round stone tower near the midpoint of the cliffs, built in 1835 by Sir Cornelius O'Brien.

facts.label: Nearest villages
facts.value: Liscannor lies 6 km to the south and Doolin 7 km to the north.

media.alt: Looking north along the Cliffs of Moher, steep layered sea cliffs above the Atlantic with O'Brien's Tower in the distance.
media.attribution: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historical capital of Bohemia. It stands on the Vltava River and is one of the larger cities in the European Union.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Capital and largest city of the Czech Republic, and historical capital of Bohemia.

facts.label: River
facts.value: The city is located on the Vltava River.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 1.4 million people, making it the twelfth-largest city in the European Union; the metropolitan area has approximately 2.3 million.

media.alt: Panoramic view of Prague from the Charles Bridge east tower, with red-roofed buildings, the river and the castle beyond.
media.attribution: Moyan Brenn, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, in the province of North Holland. It is nicknamed the "Venice of the North" for its many canals.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Capital and largest city of the Netherlands.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: As of 1 January 2026, 941,873 people lived in the city proper and 2,480,394 in the metropolitan area.

facts.label: Canals
facts.value: Its large number of canals earned it the nickname "Venice of the North", and the canals are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

media.alt: The Amsterdam skyline at night, seen from a distance.
media.attribution: Peterupton99, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Distant view of Amsterdam Skyline at night.jpg

summary.text: Florence is the capital and most populous city of the Italian region of Tuscany. It anchors a larger metropolitan area together with Prato and Pistoia.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Capital of Tuscany and of the eponymous metropolitan province.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: 361,625 people as of 2026, the eighth most populous city in Italy.

facts.label: Metropolitan area
facts.value: The Florence, Prato and Pistoia metropolitan area, constituted in 2000, covers roughly 4,800 square kilometres and is home to 1.5 million people.

media.alt: A view over the city of Florence, Italy, from Piazzale Michelangelo.
media.attribution: Giorgio Galeotti, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Firenze - Piazzale Michelangelo, Firenze, Italy - April 6, 2015 02.jpg

summary.text: Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland, in the southeast of the country. It lies between the Firth of Forth to the north and the Pentland Hills to the south.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Capital of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Bounded to the north by the Firth of Forth and to the south by the Pentland Hills.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: 506,520 in 2020, the second most populous city in Scotland and seventh in the United Kingdom; the wider metropolitan area had 912,490.

media.alt: Skyline of Edinburgh seen from Calton Hill, with historic stone buildings and spires across the city.
media.attribution: Andrew Colin, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Antarctica is Earth's southernmost and least-populated continent, lying almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle and surrounded by the Southern Ocean. It contains the geographic South Pole and is mostly covered by a vast ice sheet.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: About 14,200,000 square kilometres, making it the fifth-largest continent and roughly 40% larger than Europe.

facts.label: Ice sheet
facts.value: Most of the continent is covered by the Antarctic ice sheet, with an average thickness of 1.9 km.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: It lies almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle, is surrounded by the Southern Ocean, and contains the geographic South Pole.

media.alt: Antarctica seen from space in NASA's Blue Marble satellite composite: an ice-covered continent surrounded by ocean.
media.attribution: Dave Pape, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Antarctica 6400px from Blue Marble.jpg

summary.text: Dubai is the most populous city of the United Arab Emirates, sitting on a creek along the southeastern coast of the Persian Gulf. It grew from a small pearling and fishing settlement into a regional trade hub, and today its economy rests on trade, tourism, aviation, finance and real estate.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: Founded in the early 18th century as a pearling and fishing settlement; it became a trade hub in the 20th century after declaring itself a free port in 1901.

facts.label: Skyline
facts.value: Home to the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, as part of one of the world's densest skylines.

facts.label: Reclaimed coast
facts.value: Land-reclamation projects have added more than 300 kilometres (190 miles) of artificial coastline.

facts.label: Air hub
facts.value: Dubai International Airport is the world's busiest airport for international passenger traffic, handling over 92 million passengers in 2024.

media.alt: The Dubai skyline lit up at night.
media.attribution: Robert Bock, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Jerusalem is a city on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea. It is one of the oldest cities in the world and is holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Its political status remains disputed and is not widely settled internationally.

facts.label: Holy city
facts.value: Considered a holy city by the three major Abrahamic religions: Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

facts.label: Old City
facts.value: The walled Old City covers only about 0.9 square kilometres and has been divided since the 19th century into the Armenian, Christian, Jewish and Muslim quarters.

facts.label: City walls
facts.value: The present walls were rebuilt in 1538 under the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Old City became a World Heritage Site in 1981 and is also on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

media.alt: The golden Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem's Old City, seen across the valley from the Mount of Olives.
media.attribution: askii, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Dome of the Rock seen from the Mount of Olives (12395649153) (cropped).jpg

summary.text: The Dead Sea is a landlocked salt lake in the Jordan Rift Valley, bordered by Jordan, the West Bank and Israel. Its shores are the lowest land-based elevation on Earth, and its extreme salt content makes floating effortless. The lake has long drawn visitors and is steadily shrinking.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: As of 2025 the surface is 439.78 metres (1,443 feet) below sea level, the lowest land-based elevation on Earth.

facts.label: Salinity
facts.value: With a salinity of about 34.2% (in 2011), it is roughly 9.6 times as salty as the ocean, and its density makes swimming similar to floating.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: About 304 metres (997 feet) deep, making it the deepest hypersaline lake in the world.

facts.label: Receding shoreline
facts.value: Its surface area is about 605 square kilometres today, down from 1,050 square kilometres in 1930.

media.alt: A beach on the Jordanian shore of the Dead Sea, with parasols standing near the calm water.
media.attribution: لا روسا, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, set on the plains of Marvdasht in Iran's Fars province and ringed by the southern Zagros Mountains. Its palaces stood on a raised platform and mark a high point of Achaemenid architecture. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.label: Era
facts.value: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire (c. 550–330 BC); its earliest remains date back to 515 BC.

facts.label: Fall
facts.value: Taken by the army of Alexander the Great in 330 BC, after which its wooden parts were destroyed by fire.

facts.label: Scholarship
facts.value: Study of the site from the early 17th century led to the modern rediscovery of cuneiform writing, and its trilingual royal inscriptions helped begin the decipherment of cuneiform in the early 19th century.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

media.alt: The Tachara palace at Persepolis, a stone building with a stairway on the ancient terrace, seen from the southeast.
media.attribution: Laurens R. Krol, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — 2018-09-21 Iran, Persepolis, Tachara (from the southeast).jpg

summary.text: Wadi Rum is a valley cut into sandstone and granite in southern Jordan, close to the Saudi border and about 60 km east of Aqaba. Also called the Valley of the Moon, it is the largest wadi in Jordan, and prehistoric peoples left rock carvings and ruins there.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Covers about 720 square kilometres, making it the largest wadi (river valley) in Jordan.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in southern Jordan, about 60 km (37 miles) east of the city of Aqaba.

facts.label: Rock art
facts.value: Khaz'ali Canyon holds petroglyphs of humans and antelopes dating to Thamudic times.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Wadi Rum Protected Area has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2011.

media.alt: A sandstone mountain rising near the entrance to Wadi Rum in Jordan.
media.attribution: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Mountain in Wadi Rum, Jordan.jpg

summary.text: Karnak is a vast complex of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings near Luxor in Egypt. Work began in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic period, though most surviving structures come from the New Kingdom. It was the main place of worship of the Theban Triad, led by the god Amun.

facts.label: Long construction
facts.value: Building began under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom (305–30 BCE).

facts.label: Many builders
facts.value: Approximately thirty pharaohs contributed to the buildings, giving the site a size and diversity not seen elsewhere.

facts.label: Great Hypostyle Hall
facts.value: The hall in the Precinct of Amun-Re covers 5,000 square metres and holds 134 massive columns arranged in 16 rows.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 along with the rest of ancient Thebes.

media.alt: Ruins of the Karnak temple complex at Luxor, Egypt.
media.attribution: Hamerani, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Abu Simbel is a site of two massive rock-cut temples in Upper Egypt, on the western bank of Lake Nasser near the Sudanese border. Carved in the 13th century BC during the reign of Ramesses II, the temples are known for the colossal figures of the pharaoh on their facade. In 1968 the whole complex was moved to higher ground to save it from the rising lake.

facts.label: Two temples
facts.value: The Great Temple is dedicated to Ramesses II himself, and the Small Temple to his chief wife, Queen Nefertari.

facts.label: Relocation
facts.value: The complex was relocated in its entirety in 1968 to higher ground to avoid being submerged by Lake Nasser, as part of the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia.

facts.label: Rediscovery
facts.value: Covered over time by a sand dune, the temples remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the small temple and the top frieze of the main temple.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: About 230 km (140 miles) southwest of Aswan, on the western bank of Lake Nasser.

media.alt: Rock-cut temple facade at Abu Simbel in Aswan Governorate, southern Egypt.
media.attribution: youssef_alam, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons — Ramsis, Aswan Governorate, Egypt - panoramio.jpg

summary.text: Milford Sound is a fiord on the south-west coast of New Zealand's South Island. It lies inside Fiordland National Park and is part of the Te Wahipounamu World Heritage area. It is widely regarded as one of the country's best-known visitor destinations.

facts.label: Protected areas
facts.value: Sits within Fiordland National Park, Piopiotahi Marine Reserve and the Te Wahipounamu World Heritage site.

facts.label: Landform
facts.value: A fiord on the south-west coast of New Zealand's South Island.

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Most visitors arrive by road on tour coaches; the road ends at a small village also named Milford Sound.

facts.label: Reputation
facts.value: Rudyard Kipling is recorded as calling it the eighth Wonder of the World.

summary.text: Tongariro National Park lies in the central North Island of New Zealand and is the country's oldest national park. Three active volcanoes rise at its centre, and several of its summits are sacred to Māori. UNESCO recognises it for both its natural and cultural values.

facts.label: Park history
facts.value: The oldest national park in New Zealand and the sixth national park established in the world.

facts.label: Volcanoes
facts.value: The active volcanic mountains Ruapehu, Ngauruhoe and Tongariro stand in the centre of the park.

facts.label: Cultural significance
facts.value: Many summits, including Ngauruhoe and Ruapehu, are tapu (sacred) to Māori.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site for mixed cultural and natural values.

summary.text: Kakadu National Park is a large protected area in Australia's Northern Territory, to the south-east of Darwin. It is listed as a World Heritage Site. The park is also officially recognised as a locality with its own small resident population.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: In the Northern Territory of Australia, 171 km (106 mi) south-east of Darwin.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Kakadu is a World Heritage Site.

facts.label: Population
facts.value: Gazetted as a locality covering the same area as the park; 313 people were recorded living there in the 2016 Australian census.

summary.text: Fiji is an island country in the Melanesia region of the South Pacific Ocean. It is made up of hundreds of islands and many smaller islets, and lies roughly 1,100 nautical miles north-north-east of New Zealand.

facts.label: Islands
facts.value: More than 330 islands, of which about 110 are permanently inhabited, plus more than 500 islets.

facts.label: Land area
facts.value: About 18,300 square kilometres (7,100 sq mi).

facts.label: Population
facts.value: About 87% of people live on the two main islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: Suva, on the coast of Viti Levu.

summary.text: Bora Bora is an island group in the Leeward Islands of French Polynesia, in the South Pacific. The main island is ringed by a lagoon and a barrier reef, and its centre holds the remains of an extinct volcano.

facts.label: Land area
facts.value: About 30.55 km² (12 sq mi).

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The main island lies about 230 kilometres north-west of Papeete.

facts.label: Lagoon and reef
facts.value: The main island is surrounded by a lagoon and a barrier reef.

facts.label: Highest point
facts.value: 727 m (2,385 ft), among the twin peaks of Mount Pahia and Mount Otemanu on an extinct volcano.

summary.text: Aoraki / Mount Cook is the highest mountain in New Zealand, standing in the Southern Alps of the South Island. It is a popular destination for visitors and a favoured challenge for mountaineers.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Listed as 3,724 metres as of 2014.

facts.label: Summits
facts.value: Three summits, from south to north: Low Peak, Middle Peak and High Peak.

facts.label: Glaciers
facts.value: The Tasman Glacier lies to the east and the Hooker Glacier to the south-west.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: Ranked 10th in the world by topographic isolation.
